# Unitary dynamics, quenches, and exact limits {#sec-unitary}

## What does a quench measure?

A quantum quench changes a Hamiltonian on a timescale short compared with the
subsequent dynamics. It prepares a state that is generally not an eigenstate of
the new Hamiltonian. A global quench changes parameters throughout the system;
a local quench changes them in a finite region. These protocols inject different
amounts of energy and need not share an entanglement-growth law.

We will derive the spectral description of a quench, distinguish dephasing from
dissipation, and solve a broad class of free-particle problems. Only elementary
unitary evolution and matrix diagonalization are assumed. Later descriptions
such as ETH or hydrodynamics must agree with these exact limits where their
domains overlap.

## Spectral evolution and the diagonal ensemble

Let $H|n\rangle=E_n|n\rangle$ and
$|\psi(0)\rangle=\sum_n c_n|n\rangle$. Then

$$
\langle O(t)\rangle=\sum_{mn}c_m^*c_n
e^{i(E_m-E_n)t}O_{mn}.
$$ {#eq-unitary-spectral}

At finite dimension this is a finite sum of oscillations. It is generally
quasiperiodic and need not have a pointwise limit as $t\to\infty$. An
infinite-time average is a different object. Since the time average of
$e^{i\omega t}$ vanishes for nonzero $\omega$,

$$
\overline\rho=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\rho(t)dt
=\sum_E P_E\rho(0)P_E.
$$ {#eq-unitary-dephased}

Here $P_E$ projects onto the full degenerate energy subspace. For a
nondegenerate spectrum this becomes the diagonal ensemble
$\rho_{\mathrm{D}}=\sum_n|c_n|^2|n\rangle\langle n|$. Degenerate coherences
must not be discarded. No information has been destroyed by actual evolution;
time averaging deliberately loses phase resolution.

Dephasing can make a local observable almost constant for most times even
though the complete state remains far from a Gibbs density matrix. Thermalization
further asks whether the near-stationary local value agrees with a thermal
ensemble fixed by conserved quantities. Integrable chains provide examples
where dephasing occurs but the thermal ensemble is wrong.

## Time scales and noncommuting limits

There may be a local relaxation time, a transport time across the sample, a
Heisenberg time $t_H\sim2\pi/\delta E$ associated with mean level spacing,
and much longer recurrence times. These are distinct. For diffusion the sample
time is $L^2/D$; for a ballistic front it is $L/v$. A small chain can reach its
boundary before a proposed hydrodynamic regime develops.

An irreversible thermodynamic statement usually takes $L\to\infty$ before
$t\to\infty$ for a fixed local observable. A numerical calculation fixes
$L$ first and can only test a finite window. A narrow time average may retain
oscillations; a very broad average may wash out a physically interesting
prethermal plateau. State the averaging procedure as part of the observable.

For a nondegenerate energy-gap spectrum one can bound temporal fluctuations by
an effective dimension
$d_{\mathrm{eff}}=(\sum_n|c_n|^4)^{-1}$. The mechanism is cancellation among many
frequencies, not decay of the coefficients $c_n$. Its assumptions and ETH's
additional content are developed in [chapter 6](06-equilibration-eth.qmd).

## Heisenberg and Schrödinger pictures

Moving time dependence to operators gives
$O(t)=e^{iHt}Oe^{-iHt}$ and $\dot O=i[H,O]$. Iterating the commutator yields

$$
O(t)=O+it[H,O]+\frac{(it)^2}{2!}[H,[H,O]]+\cdots.
$$ {#eq-unitary-commutators}

Each commutator with a local Hamiltonian can enlarge spatial support by a
bounded amount. This expansion connects the spectrum to locality without
diagonalization. In a time-dependent Hamiltonian the propagator is time ordered:
$U(t)=\mathcal T\exp[-i\int_0^tH(s)ds]$. Replacing it by the exponential of
the integral is valid only when the Hamiltonians commute at different times,
or as an explicitly controlled approximation.

Linear response uses a small perturbation to the initial evolution;
scrambling uses noncommutativity of evolved and distant operators; Floquet
theory groups the propagator into periods. They are different reorganizations
of the same operator algebra.

## Exact number-conserving Gaussian dynamics

Consider $H=\sum_{ij}c_i^\dagger h_{ij}c_j$, with $h=h^\dagger$. From the
anticommutation relations,
$i\dot c_i=[c_i,H]=\sum_jh_{ij}c_j$. Therefore
$c(t)=U(t)c(0)$, where $U(t)=e^{-iht}$. Define the one-body matrix with
the explicit index convention $C_{ij}=\langle c_j^\dagger c_i\rangle$.
Then

$$
C(t)=U(t)C(0)U^\dagger(t).
$$ {#eq-unitary-correlation}

The formula for $C$ holds even for a non-Gaussian initial state, because the
operator evolution is linear. A Gaussian state has the further property that
all higher correlation functions follow from $C$ by Wick factorization. A
Slater determinant is a pure number-conserving Gaussian state with $C^2=C$.
Interacting evolution generally generates connected higher correlations, so
evolving $C$ alone ceases to determine the full state.

For a region $A$, diagonalize its restricted matrix $C_A$:
$C_A=W\operatorname{diag}(\nu_a)W^\dagger$. The associated independent
fermionic modes have occupation probabilities $\nu_a$. Consequently

$$
S_A=\sum_a[-\nu_a\ln\nu_a-(1-\nu_a)\ln(1-\nu_a)],
\qquad
S_{2,A}=-\sum_a\ln[\nu_a^2+(1-\nu_a)^2].
$$ {#eq-unitary-gaussian-entropy}

This is exact for a number-conserving Gaussian state. Pairing requires a Nambu
or Majorana covariance matrix; inserting a paired state's ordinary $C_A$ into
this formula can give a wrong entropy.

## Worked example: a density wave in the XX chain

Take the infinite hopping chain with dispersion $\epsilon(k)=J\cos k$ and
initial occupations $n_j(0)=[1+(-1)^j]/2$. The propagator follows by Fourier
transformation:

$$
U_{j\ell}(t)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{dk}{2\pi}
e^{ik(j-\ell)-iJt\cos k}=(-i)^{j-\ell}\mathcal J_{j-\ell}(Jt),
$$ {#eq-unitary-bessel}

where $\mathcal J_r$ is a Bessel function. Then
$n_j(t)=\sum_\ell|U_{j\ell}(t)|^2n_\ell(0)$. Using the Bessel identity
$\sum_r(-1)^r\mathcal J_r(x)^2=\mathcal J_0(2x)$ gives the staggered imbalance

$$
\mathcal I(t)=\frac1L\sum_j(-1)^j[2n_j(t)-1]
=\mathcal J_0(2Jt).
$$ {#eq-unitary-imbalance}

It decays with an oscillatory $t^{-1/2}$ envelope. The occupations of momentum
modes remain exactly conserved, so this relaxation is not evidence for generic
thermalization. At finite $L$, use the discrete sum and expect boundary or
recurrence effects. Comparing that sum with a full many-body calculation is
an excellent convention check.

## Pairing and the Ising mode problem

The Pauli Ising Hamiltonian
$H=-J\sum_jX_jX_{j+1}-Jg\sum_jZ_j$ becomes quadratic with pairing under
Jordan–Wigner transformation. In each $(k,-k)$ even-parity subspace a choice of
basis phase gives

$$
\mathsf h_k(g)=2J[(g-\cos k)\tau_z+\sin k\,\tau_x],
\quad \epsilon_k(g)=2J\sqrt{1+g^2-2g\cos k}.
$$ {#eq-unitary-ising-mode}

The Pauli matrices $\tau$ act on empty and paired states of these two modes.
Define a Bogoliubov angle by
$\cos2\theta_k=(g-\cos k)/[\epsilon_k/(2J)]$ and
$\sin2\theta_k=\sin k/[\epsilon_k/(2J)]$. The word Bogoliubov means a
linear transformation mixing particle creation and annihilation operators to
diagonalize a paired quadratic Hamiltonian.

Quench from a ground state at $g_i$ to $g_f$. Relative to the final ground
state, the probability of exciting the pair is
$n_k=\sin^2(\theta_k^f-\theta_k^i)$. This follows from the overlap of two
spin-one-half eigenvectors pointing along the respective mode fields. The
Loschmidt amplitude, the overlap with the initial state after evolution,
factorizes:

$$
\mathcal G(t)=\prod_{k>0}
\left[\cos(\epsilon_k^f t)
+i\cos(2\theta_k^f-2\theta_k^i)\sin(\epsilon_k^f t)\right].
$$ {#eq-unitary-loschmidt}

An irrelevant overall phase depends on energy-zero convention. The modulus
and return rate do not. This exact formula leads to dynamical quantum phase
transitions, but a singular extensive overlap is not automatically a singular
local observable [@heyl2013dqpt]. [Chapter 27](27-critical-dynamics.qmd) explains
the conditions and derives the critical times.

## Connecting exact dynamics to research

Cold-atom experiments detect propagating correlations after a global quench
[@cheneau2012lightcone]. The conceptual comparison is with correlated
quasiparticle pairs and finite propagation speeds, not with literal relativistic
causality. The measured correlation cone can have a pair-separation speed
different from a single excitation's velocity. Entanglement experiments further
show how a pure preparation can yield approximately thermal local behavior
[@kaufman2016thermalization]. Neither observation alone proves every clause of
ETH or excludes all alternative long-time ensembles.

Exact Gaussian models remain valuable at the frontier: they benchmark
algorithms, separate dephasing from collisions, and expose which conclusions
require interactions. Their efficient simulation is a structural property, not
an excuse to treat interacting systems as weakly corrected free particles
without a small parameter.

## Exercises and worked solutions

1. A two-level system has energies $\pm\omega/2$ and initial state
   $(|+\rangle+|-\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Compute a nonstationary observable, its
   time average, and the full-state trace distance to its dephased state. Does
   the state approach that average?
2. Derive the dephased density matrix when two energies are exactly degenerate.
   Compare with a splitting $\delta$ observed for $T\ll1/\delta$ and
   $T\gg1/\delta$.
3. Derive the Gaussian entropy formula by diagonalizing a two-mode reduced
   density operator with occupations $\nu_1,\nu_2$.
4. Use the Julia code in the laboratory to compare finite-chain density-wave
   imbalance with the infinite-chain Bessel result. Explain the earliest
   deviations as a function of $L$ and boundary conditions.
5. Derive the excitation probability for an Ising quench from the dot product
   of the two mode-field unit vectors. Identify momenta with probability one-half.

**Solution to 1.** Choosing $O=|+\rangle\langle-|+|-\rangle\langle+|$
gives $\cos\omega t$ and average zero. The dephased state is $I/2$, but
$T(\rho(t),I/2)=1/2$ for every $t$. An expectation can time-average to a
stationary value without the evolving state converging to the averaged density
matrix.

**Solution to 3.** In the independent-mode basis the four probabilities are
$(1-\nu_1)(1-\nu_2)$, $\nu_1(1-\nu_2)$, $(1-\nu_1)\nu_2$,
and $\nu_1\nu_2$. Taking minus their probability-weighted logarithm separates
into two binary entropies. The same factorization proves the formula for any
number of Gaussian modes. It relies on the factorized reduced Gaussian state,
not merely knowledge of two expectation values.
